newsitem.title: UK: New Greenpeace oil protest seen flopping.
newsitem.headline: New Greenpeace oil protest seen flopping.

text.p: Greenpeace is unlikely to score a Brent Spar style victory in its current campaign against British Petroleum's plans to develop oilfields in the Atlantic, industry analysts said on Tuesday.
Two activists from the environmental lobby group boarded a mobile BP drilling platform heading to the new Foinaven oilfield last Sunday.
By Tuesday the protesters had secured a survival capsule to the Stena Dee platform in preparation for a lengthy stay, a Greenpeace spokeswoman said.
The protest is part of a long running campaign against the development of a new oil province in deep Atlantic waters off the north Scottish coast.
But observers said the Greenpeace campaign lacks a clear focus, and after pouring huge amounts of money into the project, BP will not back down.

"The campaign is against oil exploration full stop...it's hard to see how an oil and gas company can react to that. All it can do is make its best efforts to be as environmentally friendly as possible," said Gordon Gray, an oil industry analyst at investment bank Salomon Brothers.
The occupation of the giant platform has failed to attract much attention in the British press.
The intense media interest which surrounded the Greenpeace occupation of Brent Spar in 1995 shored up public opposition to plans by Royal Dutch/Shell to dump the ageing rig at sea.
A boycott of Shell petrol stations by motorists, particularly in Germany, persuaded the Anglo-Dutch giant to change its mind.
"The Brent Spar was a very emotive issue, but this is different. If you boycott BP because they produce oil, then you should boycott them all," said Gray.
Huge differences in the amounts of money involved are also significant.

When Shell was forced to change tack over Brent Spar, it had spent around 10 million stg on the disposal plans. But BP's development costs at Foinaven are some 70 times more, at nearly 700 million pounds.

"Oil companies are much less responsive to pressure groups and consumer efforts than other industries because the investments are so high," said John Bray, a consultant at international political and business risk analysts Control Risks Group.
"Issues of reputation and image will be high on BP's list of concerns, but I don't see how it can compromise on this," he added.

Greenpeace said on Tuesday that it had sent a letter to BP asking it to suspend action on Foinaven ahead of a meeting between its executive director Peter Melchett and BP chief executive John Browne scheduled for September 1.
The group opposes all new oil developments, claiming that fossil fuels must remain in the ground if carbon dioxide emissions that cause global warming are to be curbed.
BP's 120,000 barrels per day Foinaven field is set to be the first of the Atlantic fields to start producing, but Greenpeace says the campaign is not just aimed at one oil company.

"Clearly it's not just down to BP to take the lead on this. We have targeted lots of other oil companies and we also think that the government must take the lead on curbing fossil fuel emissions," a Greenpeace spokeswoman said.
But the absence of a scapegoat is likely to thwart Greenpeace's efforts.
"It's not straightforward because it's not BP-specific and by and large BP has been fairly widely acclaimed for its environmental practice," said Salomon Brother's Gray.
"(Greenpeace's) aim isn't clear...there's no off-the-shelf solution," said Bray of Control Risks Group.
